---
title: "Your first steps with binwise"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5,
                     out.width = "100%", dpi = 120)
```

Binning means putting numeric values into groups. Instead of using an exact
score, for example, you might use "none", "low", and "high". That can make a
comparison easier to explain. It also means treating different values within
a group as the same category.

This short tutorial walks through one example, from inspecting the groups to
adding them to a dataset. You do not need to bring your own data.

## Install the package

Open RStudio and run these lines in the **Console**. You only need to install
the package once, unless you want to update it.

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("preblek/binwise")
```

binwise needs R 4.1 or later. It is not yet on CRAN, so
`install.packages("binwise")` is not the installation command for this version.

## Load an example

Run the following code after installing. `library()` loads the package for
this R session. `data()` loads a small example included with it.

```{r load-example}
library(binwise)
data("binwise_zero", package = "binwise")
head(binwise_zero)
```

The example describes a fictional participation score. A score of zero means
no participation; positive scores describe how much someone participates.

`head()` shows the first few rows. Each row is an observation, and `score` is
the column we will group. The example has 1,000 observations in total.

If you are new to RStudio, choose **File > New File > R Script** and copy the
code blocks into that script. Select one block at a time and press
**Command+Enter** on a Mac or **Ctrl+Enter** on Windows. Run the blocks in order.

## Look at the proposed groups

We will give zero its own category and divide the positive scores into three
groups with roughly equal counts.

```{r inspect-groups}
groups <- bin_diagnose(
  binwise_zero, "score", bins = 3,
  separate_zero = TRUE, warn = FALSE
)
groups$bins
```

`<-` saves the result under the name `groups`. The quotation marks around
`"score"` tell the function which column to use. `groups$bins` opens the table
of categories inside that saved result.

Read the table one row at a time. The lower and upper values describe a
category's boundaries. `n` tells you how many observations it contains.
There are 400 zeros, followed by three positive-score groups of 200 each.
The `bins = 3` setting applies to the positive values, so there are four
categories altogether.

```{r count-check, include=FALSE}
stopifnot(identical(as.integer(groups$bins$n), c(400L, 200L, 200L, 200L)))
```

Print the whole result to see the package's written assessment.

```{r assessment}
groups
```

The assessment points out features worth checking. It cannot tell you what
zero means in your research. That interpretation comes from your question
and your knowledge of the variable.

## Compare another way of grouping the values

Perhaps you would rather use intervals of the same width. Compare both choices
before deciding.

```{r compare-groups}
choices <- bin_compare(
  binwise_zero, "score", bins = 3,
  methods = c("quantile", "equal_width"), separate_zero = TRUE
)
plot(
  choices, type = "boundaries", show_counts = TRUE,
  xlab = "Participation score", main = "What goes into each group?",
  scheme_labels = c(quantile_3 = "Similar counts", equal_width_3 = "Equal widths")
)
```

Each horizontal segment shows the range covered by a group. The counts tell
you how many observations fall in it. Similar counts do not necessarily mean
similar ranges. Equal widths do not necessarily mean similar counts.

Use **Plots > Zoom** in RStudio if the labels look small. Orange marks identify
groups that fall below the package's count or proportion screening rules.
They are a prompt to look more closely, not an automatic rejection of the bins.

## Add the chosen categories to your data

Suppose you choose the groups from the first step. `bin_apply()` adds them as
a new column and keeps the original score.

```{r apply-groups}
with_groups <- bin_apply(
  binwise_zero, groups, name = "participation_group"
)
head(with_groups)
table(with_groups$participation_group)
```

`binwise_zero` is unchanged. `with_groups` is a new data frame containing the
original columns and `participation_group`. The groups use the exact boundaries
saved in `groups`.

## What should you conclude?

Separating no participation from some participation has a clear meaning in
this example. That is a reason to consider a separate zero category. It is
not, by itself, a reason to turn all positive values into low, medium, and
high groups.

Ask what you want to compare. If the amount of participation matters, keeping
the exact scores may be more useful. If you do choose groups, describe their
boundaries and keep the original score available.

## Where to go next

The [example gallery](example-gallery.html) shows several different situations,
including one where bins improve predictions and one where they hide a smooth
relationship. The [longer tutorial](getting-started.html) walks through model
comparisons and explains their output.

For your own data, replace `binwise_zero` with your data frame and `"score"`
with the name of your numeric column. You can also choose your own boundaries.
For example, the code below would divide a score known to run from 0 to 100
at 25, 50, and 75. Change both the data name and the boundaries for your setting.

```{r own-boundaries, eval=FALSE}
my_groups <- bin_diagnose(
  my_data, "score", method = "custom",
  breaks = c(0, 25, 50, 75, 100)
)
```

Values at an interior boundary join the interval below it. For example, 25
joins the first interval. The function help explains missing values and values
outside your chosen range.
